section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: The ideas represented in the excerpt above were most reflected in American policy in the 20th century through

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

stimulus.text_stimulus: Paraphrased excerpt (facts and statistics only; not a quotation) — “1864: Lincoln v. McClellan,” Harpweek.com: About 78 percent of the Union electorate cast ballots in 1864. Lincoln won reelection in an Electoral College landslide, 212 votes to McClellan’s 21, and took about 55 percent of the popular vote — the third-largest share of the nineteenth century. McClellan carried only New Jersey, Delaware, and Kentucky. Lincoln’s coalition drew heavily on native-born farmers, skilled and professional workers, voters of New England descent, younger voters, and military personnel (he won an estimated 78 percent of the Union soldier and sailor vote); Democrats ran strongest in the cities and among Irish- and German-American voters. Republicans also widened their congressional majorities (149 to 42 in the House, 42 to 10 in the Senate), retook several state legislatures, and lost only the New Jersey governorship.

stimulus.text: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. items.stem: Which one of the following was a consequence of the liberal successes of the 1960s?

stimulus.text: “The challenge of the next half century is whether we have the wisdom to use wealth to enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization…. The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community. It is a place where man can renew contact with nature. It is a place which honors creation for its own sake and for what it adds to the understanding of the race. It is a place where men are more concerned with the quality of their goals than the quantity of their goods. But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Excerpt 1: Historian Andrew Hacker argues the Revolution cannot be understood apart from English imperial economic policy, which had aimed since Cromwell's era at protecting English capitalist interests. When colonial economic competition jeopardized those interests, London insisted only where fundamental mercantile principles were at stake. The struggle, in this view, was not truly about taxation powers or natural rights but about the survival of English mercantile capitalism within the imperial system. (Paraphrased from Andrew Hacker, The Triumph of American Capitalism, 1940.) Excerpt 2: Historian Bernard Bailyn argues that the language of 'slavery,' 'corruption,' and 'conspiracy' in Revolutionary writing was not mere propaganda. Used forcefully across social classes, positions, and denominations, these words reflected genuine fear and anxiety: colonists sincerely believed a comprehensive conspiracy against liberty — nourished by corruption, with American oppression its most visible part — lay at the heart of British policy. (Paraphrased from Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, 1967.)
parts: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Hacker's and Bailyn's historical interpretations of the American Revolution.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development during the period 1754 to 1783 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Hacker's interpretation.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development during the period 1754 to 1783 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Bailyn's interpretation.
exemplar: Hacker offers an economic interpretation: the Revolution was a struggle to preserve English mercantile capitalism against colonial competition, not a battle of constitutional ideas. Bailyn offers an ideological interpretation: colonists genuinely feared a deliberate conspiracy against liberty, and that fear — not economics — drove the Revolution.

Parliament's post-1763 revenue program — the Sugar Act (1764) and Stamp Act (1765), designed to make colonists pay for imperial defense and administration — supports Hacker's economic reading: the flashpoints were taxes and trade regulation protecting English commercial interests.

The colonial reaction to the Coercive Acts (1774) — widely read as proof that Parliament intended to enslave America, prompting the Continental Congress and extralegal committees — supports Bailyn: colonists acted on a sincere belief in an orchestrated conspiracy against their liberties.

questions.stimulus_text: "Since the peace was made [the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne], you have kill'd some of the Shawanese, Winebagoes Delawares and Miamies and you have taken our lands from us and I do not see how we can remain at peace with you if you continue to do so. . . . We shall have a great council, at which all the tribes will be present, when we shall show to those who sold [land] that they had no right to [do so]. . . . If you will not give up the land and do cross the boundary of your present settlement, it will be very hard, and produce great troubles among us. . . . As we intend to hold our council at the Huron village, that is near the British, we may probably make them a visit. Should they offer us any presents of goods, we will not take them; but should they offer us powder and the tomahawk, we will take the powder and refuse the tomahawk." — Tecumseh, speech to Governor William Henry Harrison at Vincennes, Indiana Territory, 1810
parts: Briefly describe one likely purpose of Tecumseh in giving the speech.
Briefly explain how one historical development contributed to the circumstance discussed in the excerpt.
Briefly explain one development between 1810 and 1840 that resulted from situations such as the one depicted in the excerpt.
exemplar: Tecumseh aimed to convince Harrison that the Treaty of Fort Wayne was void — no single tribe's chiefs could sell land held in common — and to warn that if the United States kept seizing land, his united confederacy would resist by force and accept British military aid.

The 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne, in which Harrison secured some three million acres from Delaware, Miami, and Potawatomi signers, created the crisis: Tecumseh insisted those chiefs had no authority to sell shared tribal territory, so settler occupation under the treaty was, to him, theft.

The confrontation fed directly into the War of 1812, when Tecumseh allied his confederacy with Britain against the United States; his death at the Thames in 1813 shattered pan-Indian resistance in the Old Northwest and cleared the way for further American expansion.

questions.stimulus_text: The 1777 engraving shows a peaceful commercial encounter: a European trader examines a beaver pelt offered by a Native American, while another Native man smokes a long pipe nearby and a second trader leans on a barrel of trade goods. The figures face each other calmly, conducting business as willing partners.
questions.attribution: Described from a 1777 engraving of fur traders in Canada.
parts: A. Briefly explain what the engraving suggests about the nature of early contact between Europeans and Native Americans.
B. Briefly explain how one detail of the image supports your answer to part A.
C. Briefly explain one longer-term effect of the type of contact shown on Native American societies in the period 1600 to 1750.
exemplar: The engraving suggests that early contact was cooperative and commercial, presenting Europeans and Native Americans as willing trading partners.
The trader examining the beaver pelt offered by the Native trader shows voluntary commercial exchange - business between willing partners - rather than conquest or coercion.
Participation in the fur trade drew Native societies into European market economies and rivalries, intensifying inter-tribal warfare over hunting grounds and access to European goods.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: To what extent did the Federalist administrations of George Washington and John Adams promote national unity and advance the authority of the federal government in the period 1789–1801?

documents.text: "I behold the surest pledges that … no local prejudices or attachments, no separate views or party animosities, will misdirect the comprehensive and equal eye which ought to watch over [Congress] … that the foundation of our national policy will be laid in the pure and immutable principles of private morality, and the preeminence of free government be exemplified by all the attributes which can win the affections of its citizens and command the respect of the world." —George Washington, First Inaugural Address (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Washington speaks as the unifying, above-party first president addressing Congress and the nation; his purpose is to legitimize the new federal government and bind diverse states to it. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists promoted unity and federal authority—or, with Docs F/G, to show how far practice fell short of this ideal.

documents.text: "The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Virginia … represent [that] … in an agricultural country like this … to perpetuate a large monied interest, is a measure which … must … produce … the prostration of agriculture at the feet of commerce, or a change in the present form of federal government, fatal to the existence of American liberty." —Virginia Resolutions on the Assumption of State Debts (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Virginia's legislature, led by opponents of Hamilton's financial program, protests to Congress; its purpose is to block assumption of state debts as unconstitutional and sectional. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist policies divided the nation along sectional lines and expanded federal power in ways critics called dangerous to liberty.

documents.text: "I consider the foundation of the Constitution as laid on this ground—that all powers not delegated to the United States, by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the states, are reserved to the states, or to the people. To take a single step beyond the boundaries thus specially drawn around the powers of Congress, is to take possession of a boundless field of power." —Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Jefferson writes privately to Washington as secretary of state, urging a veto; his purpose is to stop Hamilton's bank and defend strict construction. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist actions advanced federal authority beyond constitutional limits—or that even the administration's own cabinet saw its authority as overreach.

documents.text: "The powers contained in a constitution of government, especially those which concern the general administration of the affairs of a country, its finances, trade, defense, etc., ought to be construed liberally in advancement of the public good." —Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Hamilton writes to Washington to justify the bank; his purpose is to establish the doctrine of implied powers and win presidential approval. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists deliberately expanded federal authority—the clearest statement of the loose-construction doctrine that built national power.

documents.text: "Whereas combinations to defeat the execution of the laws laying duties upon spirits distilled within the United States … have … existed in some of the western parts of Pennsylvania; … it is in my judgement necessary … to take measures for calling forth the militia in order to suppress the combinations aforesaid, and to cause the laws to be duly executed." —George Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Washington issues a presidential proclamation to the nation; his purpose is to justify using federal military force against domestic resistance and to demonstrate that federal law will be enforced. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists decisively advanced federal authority—the first use of national military power to enforce a federal tax—though it also bred western resentment.

documents.text: "That if any person shall write, print, utter, or publish, any false, scandalous, and malicious writing … against the government of the United States … with the intent to defame the said government, … then such person … shall be punished by a fine not exceeding two thousand dollars, and by imprisonment not exceeding two years." —The Sedition Act (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: A Federalist Congress legislates during the Quasi-War crisis; its purpose is to silence Republican opposition press and critics of Adams. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist rule undermined national unity and abused federal authority—the strongest evidence that 'advancing authority' came at liberty's expense.

documents.text: "Resolved, that the several States … are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government; … [the Sedition Act], which does abridge the freedom of the press, is not law but is altogether void." —Kentucky Resolutions (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Kentucky's legislature, secretly drafted by Jefferson, answers the Alien and Sedition Acts; its purpose is to assert states' right to judge federal overreach and rally Republican resistance. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist policies fractured national unity, provoking the nullification doctrine that would haunt the republic for decades.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which reform movements played an important role in shaping American society from 1820 to 1860.
leq.guidance: Thesis frame: argue the reach and limits of antebellum reform. Evidence buckets: Second Great Awakening as engine; abolitionism, temperance, women's rights (Seneca Falls); utopian communities and public schools; the tension between reform's moral claims and its limited victories before the Civil War.
